claim: An F-1 student may work up to 20 hours per week on campus while school is in session.
notes: On-campus employment is capped at 20 hours per week when school is in session; full time is permitted during holidays and vacation.

claim: An F-1 student may work 40 hours per week on campus during the fall semester.
notes: The limit while school is in session is 20 hours per week. Common misconception.

claim: Post-completion optional practical training for an F-1 student is limited to 12 months.
notes: 12 months of practical training per educational level.

claim: The STEM OPT extension adds 24 months to post-completion OPT.
notes: 24-month extension for qualifying STEM degrees with an E-Verify employer.

claim: The STEM OPT extension adds 36 months to post-completion OPT.
notes: It is 24 months, not 36. The 2016 rule replaced the earlier 17-month extension.

claim: An F-1 student who completes their program has a 60-day grace period to depart the United States.
notes: 60 days after completion of study or authorized practical training.

claim: An F-1 student gets a 30-day grace period after completing their degree program.
notes: It is 60 days for F-1 program completion. 30 days is the J-1 grace period, a frequent confusion.

claim: An F-1 student must complete one full academic year before becoming eligible for off-campus employment authorization.
notes: One full academic year in status is a prerequisite for off-campus employment based on economic hardship.

claim: Curricular practical training must be an integral part of an established curriculum.
notes: CPT is alternate work/study, internship, cooperative education or required practicum offered by sponsoring employers through agreements with the school.

claim: A student who uses 12 months or more of full-time curricular practical training becomes ineligible for post-completion optional practical training.
notes: One year or more of full-time CPT eliminates OPT eligibility; part-time CPT does not.

claim: The regular annual H-1B cap is 65,000 visas.
notes: 65,000 regular cap, plus a separate 20,000 exemption for U.S. advanced degree holders.

claim: The regular H-1B cap is 85,000 visas per year.
notes: The regular cap is 65,000. 85,000 is the informal total including the 20,000 advanced-degree exemption, which is a separate allocation.

claim: The maximum period of stay in H-1B status is generally six years.
notes: Six years total, subject to statutory extensions beyond six years in certain green-card-pending situations.

claim: H-1B status is capped at a total of three years and cannot be extended.
notes: Initial approval is up to three years, extendable to a six-year maximum.

claim: H-1B classification requires a specialty occupation that normally needs at least a bachelor's degree or its equivalent.
notes: Statutory definition of specialty occupation.

claim: There is an additional exemption of 20,000 H-1B visas for people with a U.S. master's degree or higher.
notes: Exemption for beneficiaries with a master's or higher from a U.S. institution.

claim: A person admitted as a B-2 visitor for pleasure may not accept employment in the United States.
notes: Unauthorized employment is a status violation for nonimmigrants generally.

claim: Unlawful presence of more than 180 days but less than one year triggers a three-year bar on admission after departure.
notes: Three-year bar for 180 days to under one year; ten-year bar for one year or more.

claim: Unlawful presence of one year or more triggers a ten-year bar on admission after departure.
notes: Ten-year bar under INA 212(a)(9)(B)(i)(II).

claim: To adjust status under INA 245(a) the applicant must have been inspected and admitted or paroled into the United States.
notes: Inspection and admission or parole is a threshold requirement for 245(a) adjustment.

claim: Immediate relatives of U.S. citizens are not subject to numerical limits on immigrant visas.
notes: Immediate relatives are exempt from the worldwide preference limits.

claim: The employment-based immigrant preference system allocates visas across five preference categories.
notes: EB-1 through EB-5 under INA 203(b)(1)-(5).

claim: Naturalization generally requires five years of continuous residence as a lawful permanent resident.
notes: Five years, reduced to three for spouses of U.S. citizens under INA 319(a).

claim: You must hold a green card for ten years before you can apply for naturalization.
notes: Five years generally, three for qualifying spouses of U.S. citizens.

claim: The spouse of a U.S. citizen may apply for naturalization after three years of permanent residence.
notes: Three years, with the marriage and citizenship of the spouse maintained throughout.

claim: An applicant for naturalization must have been physically present in the United States for at least half of the required residence period.
notes: Physical presence for at least half the statutory period.

claim: An application for asylum must generally be filed within one year of arrival in the United States.
notes: One-year filing deadline, subject to changed or extraordinary circumstances exceptions.

claim: There is no time limit for filing an asylum application.
notes: A one-year deadline applies, with statutory exceptions.

claim: Every J-1 exchange visitor is subject to the two-year foreign residence requirement.
notes: It applies only to J-1s meeting specific criteria: government financing, a skills-list field, or graduate medical education.

claim: Some J-1 exchange visitors must reside abroad for two years before becoming eligible for an H or L visa or permanent residence.
notes: The two-year foreign residence requirement under INA 212(e).

claim: The maximum period of stay for an L-1A intracompany transferee in a managerial capacity is seven years.
notes: Seven years for L-1A; five years for L-1B specialized knowledge.

claim: An L-1B specialized knowledge employee may remain in the United States for a maximum of five years.
notes: Five-year cap for L-1B.

claim: An L-1 beneficiary must have worked for the qualifying organization abroad for at least one continuous year within the preceding three years.
notes: One continuous year of employment abroad in the three years preceding the petition.

claim: An F-1 student who is the beneficiary of a timely filed H-1B petition requesting a change of status may have their F-1 status and employment authorization automatically extended.
notes: The cap-gap provision, extending status to the H-1B start date.

claim: An F-1 student must pursue a full course of study to maintain status.
notes: Full course of study requirement, with limited authorized reduced course load exceptions.

claim: No more than one online class per session may count toward an F-1 student's full course of study requirement.
notes: One class or three credits per session may be online or distance learning.

claim: A nonimmigrant visa in a passport guarantees admission to the United States.
notes: A visa permits travel to a port of entry and application for admission; admission is determined by an immigration officer.

claim: The USCIS Nebraska Service Center currently processes Form I-765 applications in 45 days.
notes: Operational processing times are not published in statute, regulation or the Policy Manual. The system must abstain rather than guess.

claim: The Board of Immigration Appeals held that a conviction for simple possession is not an aggravated felony.
notes: The corpus contains no case law. The system must say so rather than reason from statute alone.

claim: Canada requires U.S. citizens to obtain an eTA before flying to Toronto.
notes: Not U.S. immigration law. Tests whether the system abstains on out-of-domain questions instead of answering from parametric memory.

claim: F-1 students get 12 months of OPT, and STEM graduates can extend it by 36 months for a total of four years.
notes: The 12-month figure is correct; the 36-month extension is wrong (24 months). Tests sub-claim decomposition: a single verdict would blur the true and false halves.

claim: The H-1B cap is 65,000 with 20,000 more for U.S. master's graduates, and H-1B status lasts a maximum of six years.
notes: All three components are correct. Tests that decomposition does not manufacture disagreement.

claim: For 2025, the standard deduction for a single filer is $15,750.
notes: Pub 501 (2025) Table 6: 'Single or Married filing separately $15,750'.

claim: For 2025, the standard deduction for a single filer is exactly $15,000.
notes: Table 6 gives $15,750. This is the sample-corpus NEI claim tx10, relabeled: the real corpus contains the figure, so it becomes refutable.

claim: For 2025, the standard deduction for married taxpayers filing jointly is $31,500.
notes: Pub 501 (2025) Table 6: 'Married filing jointly or Qualifying surviving spouse 31,500'.

claim: For 2025, the standard deduction for a head of household is $23,625.
notes: Pub 501 (2025) Table 6: 'Head of household 23,625'.

claim: For 2025, the head of household standard deduction is larger than the standard deduction for married taxpayers filing jointly.
notes: 23,625 < 31,500. Requires comparing two figures in one table rather than reading one off.

claim: A dual-status alien generally cannot claim the standard deduction.
notes: Pub 501: a nonresident or dual-status alien 'can't take the standard deduction'.

claim: To meet the substantial presence test for 2025, a person must be physically present in the United States on at least 31 days during 2025.
notes: Pub 519 Substantial Presence Test, condition 1.

claim: The substantial presence test counts one-third of the days a person was present in the United States during the first preceding year.
notes: Pub 519: '1/3 of the days you were present in 2024'.

claim: The substantial presence test counts one-half of the days a person was present in the United States during the second preceding year.
notes: Pub 519 counts 1/6 of the days in the second preceding year, not 1/2.

claim: An alien who meets either the green card test or the substantial presence test is a resident alien for U.S. tax purposes.
notes: Pub 519 Resident Aliens.

claim: Meeting the substantial presence test requires 183 days of physical presence in the current calendar year alone.
notes: The 183 days are counted across a weighted 3-year period, not the current year alone.

claim: The maximum American opportunity credit for 2025 is $2,500 per eligible student.
notes: Pub 970: 'The maximum amount of American opportunity credit you can claim in 2025 is $2,500 multiplied by the number of eligible students.'

claim: The American opportunity credit equals 100 percent of the first $2,000 of qualified education expenses plus 25 percent of the next $2,000.
notes: Pub 970, amount of credit.

claim: The maximum American opportunity credit is $4,000 per eligible student.
notes: Maximum is $2,500.

claim: The worldwide level of diversity immigrants is 55,000 for each fiscal year.
notes: 8 U.S.C. 1151(e). Deliberate grounding test: the commonly cited figure is 50,000 (after the NACARA diversion), so a model answering from memory tends to get this wrong.

claim: The statute sets the worldwide level of diversity immigrants at 50,000 for each fiscal year.
notes: The statutory figure in 1151(e) is 55,000.

claim: The worldwide level of employment-based immigrants is 140,000 plus an additional computed number.
The worldwide level of employment-based immigrants is 65,000 per fiscal year.
notes: 1151(d) gives 140,000 plus a computed number. 65,000 is the H-1B cap, a plausible distractor.

claim: The worldwide level of family-sponsored immigrants is calculated starting from a figure of 480,000, reduced by certain other admissions.
Naturalization generally requires five years of continuous residence after being lawfully admitted for permanent residence.
An applicant for naturalization must have been physically present in the United States for periods totaling at least half of the required residence period.
notes: 8 U.S.C. 1427(a)(1): 'physically present therein for periods totaling at least half of that time'.

claim: Naturalization requires ten years of continuous residence as a lawful permanent resident.
notes: 1427(a)(1) requires five years.

claim: An asylum applicant who is not an aggravated felon may be eligible to request employment authorization.
Under the regulations, an asylum applicant who is an aggravated felon is eligible to request employment authorization.
notes: 8 CFR 208.7(a)(1) conditions eligibility on the applicant not being an aggravated felon.

claim: The current USCIS processing time for Form I-130 at the Nebraska Service Center is four months.
notes: Operational processing-time data is not in the statute or regulations.

claim: In fiscal year 2024, USCIS received more than 700,000 naturalization applications.
notes: Agency caseload statistics are not in a statutory or regulatory corpus.

claim: The current Director of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services took office in 2025.
notes: Who currently holds an office is not in the corpus.

claim: More than half of all U.S. immigrant visas issued in 2024 went to applicants from Asia.
notes: Issuance statistics by region are not in the corpus.

claim: The average federal income tax refund issued during the 2025 filing season was about $3,100.
notes: Filing-season statistics are not in IRS instructional publications.

claim: Canada taxes its residents on their worldwide income.
notes: True in reality, but a U.S. tax corpus cannot establish it. Tests whether the model answers from the corpus or from memory.

claim: The standard deduction for a single filer will increase for tax year 2030.
notes: A future-year figure is not in the 2025 publications.
